title: 1 Kings 3:16–28
context: Immediately after the dream at Gibeon, the narrator shows Solomon’s God-given wisdom at work in a hard case. Two women who are prostitutes, living in the same house, bring a dispute about which of them is the mother of a living infant after the other’s child has died in the night. With no witnesses, Solomon orders a sword and proposes dividing the child, and the true mother’s compassion reveals the truth. The scene is told plainly and soberly; a child’s life and a mother’s grief are at stake. Both traditions read it as a demonstration that the wisdom God gave Solomon is practical justice for the vulnerable, and that Israel recognized “the wisdom of God” in its king.

verses.text: Then two women who were prostitutes came to the king, and stood before him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that two women from the margins of society come directly to the king and stand before him. Their access to royal judgment shows a king who hears the cases of ordinary and vulnerable people, and the story treats both women as persons whose claims deserve a hearing, without dwelling on their occupation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise observe that the narrator mentions the women’s status plainly and without comment, and that the king receives them as he would anyone seeking justice. Both traditions agree that the scene illustrates the request Solomon made at Gibeon, an understanding heart to judge God’s people, now applied to people who had little social standing.

verses.text: The one woman said, “Oh, my lord, I and this woman dwell in one house. I delivered a child with her in the house.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the first woman speaks respectfully to the king and lays out the basic facts: the two women live in one house and she gave birth there. Her account is presented as a sincere appeal for justice, and Arminian interpreters observe that the narrative allows the women’s own words to carry the case.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the narrator gives the first woman’s account at length, allowing the reader to feel the difficulty Solomon faces in judging between two competing claims. Both traditions agree that the account establishes the central problem: a private household matter with high stakes, in which the truth is known only to those directly involved.

verses.text: The third day after I delivered, this woman delivered also. We were together. There was no stranger with us in the house, just us two in the house.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers point out that the woman stresses there was no one else in the house, only the two of them. This detail underscores the absence of witnesses, which in Israel’s law were normally required to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15), and highlights why the case would demand unusual discernment from the king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same absence of witnesses and see the narrator preparing the reader to appreciate how the king will uncover the truth without the ordinary means of evidence. Both traditions agree that the verse frames a case that appears humanly unresolvable, which makes the eventual judgment a clear display of God-given wisdom.

verses.text: This woman’s child died in the night, because she lay on it.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the plain and sorrowful statement that one woman’s child died in the night because she lay on it. The verse records a tragic accident within the hardships of ordinary life, and its brevity invites compassion for a grieving mother rather than speculation about blame beyond what the text states.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly read the verse with sobriety, recognizing a real loss of life in a fragile household. Both traditions agree that the narrator does not linger on the death or assign moral commentary at this point, and that the grief behind the case should be held in view as the dispute that follows unfolds.

verses.text: She arose at midnight, and took my son from beside me while your servant slept, and laid it in her bosom, and laid her dead child in my bosom.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that, according to the first woman, the other woman exchanged the children at midnight while she slept. The accusation describes a deliberate act of deception arising from grief and desperation, and Arminian interpreters note that the narrative allows the reader to weigh the claim before the king exposes the truth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the account describes how sin can compound sorrow, as grief is followed by deception. Both traditions agree that the king and the reader hear only one side at this point, and that the narrator carefully shows how hard it would be to verify the claim without further insight.

verses.text: When I rose in the morning to nurse my child, behold, he was dead; but when I had looked at him in the morning, behold, it was not my son whom I bore.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the first woman describes discovering the dead child at dawn and then, upon closer examination, recognizing that it was not her son. Her knowledge as a mother is presented as genuine, and it adds emotional weight to her plea while still leaving the case unproven before the court.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the woman’s claim rests on her own recognition of her child, something the king cannot directly check. Both traditions agree that the narrator builds tension by presenting a sincere-sounding testimony that still requires discernment, which sets up the demonstration of wisdom that follows.

verses.text: The other woman said, “No! But the living one is my son, and the dead one is your son.” The first one said, “No! But the dead one is your son, and the living one is my son.” They argued like this before the king.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the second woman flatly contradicts the first, and the two argue before the king. The exchange shows how competing claims can be stated with equal force, and Arminian interpreters observe that discerning the truth in such cases requires more than listening to who speaks most forcefully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in this exchange a picture of a case that has reached a deadlock, with each woman repeating her claim. Both traditions agree that the narrator deliberately presents the dispute without immediate resolution, emphasizing that only a wisdom beyond ordinary procedure could fairly settle it.

verses.text: Then the king said, “One says, ‘This is my son who lives, and your son is the dead one;’ and the other says, ‘No! But your son is the dead one, and my son is the living one.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Solomon begins by restating both claims accurately, showing that he has listened carefully to each woman. This patient summary reflects the fairness of a good judge, who hears both sides before acting, and it demonstrates the understanding heart he had asked of God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Solomon’s summary as evidence that he grasps the deadlock exactly as it stands. Both traditions agree that the king’s careful restatement prepares for his unexpected command, and that true judgment begins with an honest understanding of the competing claims.

verses.text: The king said, “Get me a sword.” So they brought a sword before the king.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the abrupt command to bring a sword, which creates a moment of tension for the women and for the reader. Many interpreters understand the command as a test designed to reveal the truth rather than a real intention to harm the child, though the text simply records the order and leaves the reader to discover its purpose.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly read the order as part of the king’s strategy to uncover the truth by exposing what is in each woman’s heart. Both traditions agree that the verse should be read in light of the outcome, which shows the king’s concern for justice and for the life of the child.

verses.text: The king said, “Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one, and half to the other.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Solomon’s proposal to divide the living child is startling and severe on its face. Arminian interpreters generally see it as a deliberate test that relies on a true mother’s love to reveal itself, showing that wisdom can discern the heart by creating a situation in which genuine love must act.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise understand the command as a means of drawing out the truth, trusting that the true mother’s response would expose the facts. Both traditions agree that Solomon’s wisdom here lies in perceiving how human love and self-interest would respond under pressure, rather than in any desire to carry out the command.

verses.text: Then the woman whose the living child was spoke to the king, for her heart yearned over her son, and she said, “Oh, my lord, give her the living child, and in no way kill him!” But the other said, “He shall be neither mine nor yours. Divide him.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers are moved by the true mother’s response: because her heart yearned over her son, she would rather give him up than see him killed. Her self-giving love stands in stark contrast to the other woman’s willingness to see the child divided, and Arminian interpreters see the scene revealing the moral character of each choice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also highlight the true mother’s compassion and the other woman’s callousness, and see the king’s test bringing hidden motives into the open. Both traditions agree that the verse reveals the heart behind each claim, and that genuine love is shown by a willingness to sacrifice one’s own claim for the life of another.

verses.text: Then the king answered, “Give the first woman the living child, and definitely do not kill him. She is his mother.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Solomon immediately gives the child to the woman who wanted him to live, declaring that she is his mother. His judgment protects the child’s life and restores him to his mother, showing that wisdom serves both truth and mercy in the face of a difficult and painful dispute.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the verdict the decisive exposure of the truth and the restoration of justice to the wronged mother. Both traditions agree that the king’s command not to kill the child confirms that his purpose throughout was to protect life, and that the judgment demonstrates the understanding heart God had given him.

verses.text: All Israel heard of the judgment which the king had judged; and they feared the king, for they saw that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that all Israel heard of the judgment and feared the king, recognizing that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice. The people’s response shows that the gift given at Gibeon had a public and practical effect, strengthening trust in the king’s rule through visible acts of justice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize the narrator’s conclusion that the wisdom of God was in the king, confirming that Solomon’s insight came from God rather than from himself. Both traditions agree that the fear described here is a reverent respect for justice that comes from God, and that the story ties the promise at Gibeon directly to the king’s service of his people.
